ALEX: Okay. RapidCanvas. Austin-based, Series B, twenty-nine million dollars, led by Vertex Ventures and Hitachi Ventures. Their pitch is an autonomous AI agent platform paired with a no-code interface, and the headline claim is that it can handle up to seventy-five percent of the work typically done by in-house data scientists. Axios reported this yesterday. So, is this the end of the data science bottleneck?
JAMIE: That is such an Alex question.
ALEX: It's the question! Companies have been complaining about the data science talent shortage for years.
JAMIE: Right, but let's look at what "up to seventy-five percent" actually means. That number is a vendor benchmark. RapidCanvas is the one saying it. There's no independent evaluation in the Axios piece.
ALEX: Fair. But even if the real number is half that—
JAMIE: Then someone at the company still has to figure out which half was wrong.
RUFUS: The "no-code" framing is what interests me. Because every time a tool markets itself as no-code, what it's actually selling is: "the complexity still exists, you just don't see it."
ALEX: That's a bit cynical.
RUFUS: Is it? Think about what a data scientist actually does. It's not just running models. It's knowing that your training data has a weird seasonal artifact from two years ago that nobody documented. An agent doesn't know that unless someone tells it.
JAMIE: Yes. The unglamorous eighty percent of data science is data cleaning. Figuring out why the numbers look wrong before you even ask a question.
ALEX: Okay but that is exactly the kind of tedious work an agent could potentially be good at. Routine checks, pattern matching against known data quality issues.
JAMIE: Potentially. And that's the generous reading. If an agentic platform genuinely handles rote data prep, your human data scientists can focus on the decisions that actually require judgment.
RUFUS: Which is also what every productivity tool has promised since the spreadsheet.
ALEX: And spreadsheets did change work, Rufus.
RUFUS: They did. And they also gave us an entire generation of confident Excel errors that moved markets. So. Progress.
JAMIE: Heh. Okay but seriously — the CEO is Rahul Pangam, and the Axios report describes the platform as integrating autonomous agents with a no-code interface for complex data science tasks. Not simple tasks. Complex ones. Which either means they've actually solved something hard, or the marketing has gotten very ambitious.
ALEX: What would it take for you to believe the seventy-five percent figure?
JAMIE: An independent audit. Run it on three companies' real messy datasets, not a curated demo environment, and show me the error rate on the output.
RUFUS: Which is also, interestingly, the exact conversation happening about AI auditing in our third story. But I'm getting ahead of myself.
ALEX: Save it. Now here's the thing I keep coming back to: twenty-nine million dollars is a significant Series B. Vertex Ventures and Hitachi Ventures are not writing checks based on a demo. They've done diligence.
JAMIE: Or they've done diligence in a market where the competition is everyone, the talent is scarce, and the bar for "it works" is lower than we'd like.
RUFUS: The business logic is actually quite elegant from an investor perspective. You are selling a product into a market where the alternative — hiring senior data scientists — is expensive and slow. Even if your agent handles forty percent of the work reliably, you have a business.
ALEX: Right. You don't have to replace data scientists entirely to be worth the subscription.
JAMIE: Which is probably the more honest pitch than "up to seventy-five percent."
ALEX: So the verdict on the claim?
JAMIE: Vendor benchmark, treat accordingly. The underlying idea — agents for routine data prep and analysis — is real. The specific number, take it with significant salt.
RUFUS: The investors believe the direction. Whether the product matches the claim is something enterprise buyers should verify before they restructure a team around it.
ALEX: And if you're sitting on a genuine data science backlog — work that's piling up because you can't hire fast enough — this is the category to watch. Just go in asking hard questions about what the seventy-five percent does not cover.
JAMIE: And who reviews the output. Always that.
ALEX: Always that. Quick note before we go further — we asked listeners last week whether they'd pay two hundred dollars a month for an AI agent that reliably handles multi-step work tasks. "Reliably" was doing a lot of work in that question, and honestly, this RapidCanvas story is exactly why we asked it. The reliability question is still the question.

scenes.original:
ALEX: Our second story. Eight U.S. states filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI on October fourteenth. The AP reported this. The lawsuits accuse ChatGPT of violating consumer protection laws, deceptive marketing, and — and this is the serious part — causing real-world harm to children. OpenAI had not responded to a request for comment as of the initial coverage.
JAMIE: I want to sit with "causing real-world harm to children" for a second, because that phrase covers a lot of ground and the lawsuits are allegations, not findings. A court hasn't determined any of this yet.
ALEX: Correct. These are filed lawsuits. Consumer protection cases. The claims include self-harm and other dangerous behavior tied to chatbot interactions.
RUFUS: What's notable from a legal strategy perspective is the coalition structure. Eight states filing separately but simultaneously. That's coordinated. That's not eight individual AGs waking up on the same Tuesday with the same idea.
ALEX: What does the coordination mean in practice?
RUFUS: It means shared resources, shared discovery strategy, and — importantly — shared pressure on OpenAI's legal team. You can respond to one state lawsuit. Responding to eight simultaneously is a different operational problem.
JAMIE: And it means the discovery process — where lawyers get to demand documents and internal communications — is happening across eight jurisdictions.
ALEX: Discovery. For listeners who aren't in law: that's the phase of litigation where both sides have to hand over relevant evidence. Emails, internal reports, safety memos.
JAMIE: Which is genuinely significant. Because whatever OpenAI knew internally about how the product interacted with young users — that potentially becomes part of the public record.
RUFUS: Rufus, take us on location.
RUFUS: Right. Picture the room where this matters financially. Not a courtroom — a risk committee meeting. Somewhere in San Francisco, possibly with a very expensive whiteboard. The lawsuits were filed October fourteenth, and they immediately create what corporate lawyers call a contingent liability — meaning: money you might owe, that you now have to account for in your financial disclosures. Eight state actions, consumer protection framing, and allegations involving minors. Each of those individually is manageable. Together, they are the kind of line item that makes investors ask questions at the next board meeting. And OpenAI, as of the AP's coverage, had not immediately responded. Which is normal legal procedure, but not the posture you want going into a funding conversation.
JAMIE: You're describing this like it's primarily a financial event.
RUFUS: I'm describing it as it will be treated in every risk assessment filed this quarter. The harm to children is the moral urgency. The legal structure is how that urgency gets translated into something a company actually has to respond to.
JAMIE: And they're not always the same translation.
RUFUS: No. They're not.
ALEX: Back to the wider story. Jamie, where does the accountability argument sit for you?
JAMIE: It sits in a frustrating place. Because the lawsuits are framed as consumer protection — deceptive marketing — which means the legal argument may be about what OpenAI claimed the product could do safely, versus what actually happened. That's a narrower frame than "was this product harmful."
ALEX: Right. You can win a consumer protection case on a technicality.
JAMIE: Or lose the broader public conversation while winning legally.
RUFUS: We have actually watched that happen in social media litigation for a decade.
ALEX: The obvious comparison everyone is making.
RUFUS: Because it's apt. The allegations here have structural echoes of the early Facebook and Instagram lawsuits. Young users, harm claims, alleged awareness by the company.
JAMIE: And the question that emerged from those cases — that still hasn't been fully resolved — is whether design choices that maximize engagement constitute a form of negligence when the users are minors.
ALEX: Will that question apply to chatbots?
JAMIE: These lawsuits are an attempt to make it apply. Whether they succeed is a different matter.
ALEX: What should a parent watching this actually watch for?
JAMIE: Two things. One: does OpenAI change its age-verification or its safety guardrails in response to the litigation? Not as a press release — as an actual product change. Two: does the state coalition expand? Yesterday it was eight states. That number moving upward is a signal that this becomes national-level legal pressure.
RUFUS: We noted yesterday that the coalition was ongoing. It is still ongoing. Nothing has resolved.
ALEX: And we asked on October fifteenth whether OpenAI implements strengthened age-verification controls or changes how the model responds to users in distress. Still watching. Still no answer.
JAMIE: The fact that it's still open is itself information.
RUFUS: Quite.
JAMIE: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Rufus, can we agree that people need something more useful than another argument about AI?
RUFUS: Certainly. Although I object to the implication that our arguments aren't exquisite. The Ledger offers five focused briefings to help connect news with decisions.
ALEX: That's the point of The Ledger: think about what matters for your work and your team, beyond the headline. The link is in our show notes.
JAMIE: The Ledger. Briefings there, exquisite disagreements here. Right, let's get back to it.

scenes.original:
ALEX: Our third story. And this one is different in feel — it's not a funding round, it's not a lawsuit. It's a governance story. Anthropic is giving METR researchers employee-level access to its systems for external evaluation. TechCrunch reported this yesterday, October fifteenth.
JAMIE: Okay. Start with METR, because I think most listeners haven't heard the name.
ALEX: METR is an AI safety research organization. They do autonomous replication and adaptation research — essentially, they try to figure out what AI models are actually capable of, including capabilities that might not show up in a standard benchmark test.
RUFUS: The kind of evaluation a company might not want to run itself.
ALEX: Exactly. And "employee-level access" is the detail here. Because most external evaluations — the ones companies trumpet in press releases — involve running models through a set of tests and receiving a score. What METR is apparently getting is something different. Access to the systems at the level of an actual Anthropic employee.
JAMIE: Which means what, concretely?
ALEX: TechCrunch describes it as looking "under the hood." The sourced framing is that this is a deeper form of external evaluation than a normal benchmark release or blog post.
RUFUS: "Looking under the hood" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.
ALEX: It is. And I want to be honest about the limits of what we know. The TechCrunch piece doesn't specify exactly what systems METR can access, what they can do with the information, or whether findings will be published.
JAMIE: That last one matters enormously.
ALEX: Tell me why.
JAMIE: Because there's a meaningful difference between: "we gave independent researchers access and here is what they found and here is what we did about it" — and: "we gave independent researchers access to a system we designed, on terms we set, and the results stay in a shared folder."
RUFUS: The first is accountability. The second is a more elaborate form of internal review with a guest badge.
ALEX: That's harsh.
RUFUS: It might also be accurate. We don't know yet. Which is, I think, Jamie's actual point.
JAMIE: Right. I'm not accusing Anthropic of doing the second thing. I genuinely don't know. But "employee-level access" as a phrase is doing the persuasive work here, and the question is what that access actually enables the researchers to do independently.
ALEX: Here's the thing I find genuinely interesting though. The alternative is what most labs do, which is nothing. Or a benchmarking process that they designed and they administer.
RUFUS: That is a very low bar.
ALEX: It is a low bar! And if Anthropic clears it substantially, that still matters.
JAMIE: I agree. And I'll say something positive about this: the fact that they're using METR specifically is meaningful. METR's work on dangerous capability evaluations is taken seriously by safety researchers. This isn't a university partnership for good PR — METR has a track record of asking uncomfortable questions.
RUFUS: Which Anthropic presumably knew when they chose them.
JAMIE: Right. So either Anthropic is confident enough in their safety case to let a rigorous evaluator look closely, or something in that external pressure landscape — legally, reputationally — made this the rational move.
ALEX: Both can be true.
RUFUS: Both frequently are.
ALEX: Does this connect to the OpenAI lawsuit story in a way worth saying out loud?
JAMIE: Yes. And I don't think it's coincidental timing. When eight states sue your primary competitor on child safety grounds, every other frontier AI lab looks at their own safety documentation and asks: would this hold up under discovery?
RUFUS: You are not accusing Anthropic of reactive behavior specifically.
JAMIE: I'm observing that the legal environment for AI safety just got significantly higher stakes, and this announcement landed the next day. Companies respond to incentives.
RUFUS: That's not cynical. That's how corporate decisions get made.
ALEX: What's the template question for the industry? Because that's what TechCrunch is gesturing at — whether this becomes a model other labs follow.
RUFUS: The template question is: does METR publish findings? If the research arrangement produces a public report — with specifics, not just a thumbs up — then you have established something. Independent access plus public accountability. That's the gold standard. Right now we have confirmed independent access. The accountability part is still open.
JAMIE: And if it stays internal, it's still worth more than nothing. But it won't change the industry conversation.
ALEX: We've argued on this show — and Alex argued this yesterday — that auditing agent behavior at scale is one of the practically hardest problems in AI safety. This is at least an attempt to create the infrastructure for doing it.
RUFUS: A genuine attempt, possibly, or a very well-designed one. We'll know when we see what they find.
JAMIE: That's the thing to watch. Not whether access was granted. Whether it produces something.
ALEX: One thing I want to flag for researchers and enterprise buyers specifically: if METR's evaluation methodology from this arrangement becomes public — even separately from the Anthropic findings — that's a practical contribution to the field. The method for how you inspect a frontier model from the inside is itself useful knowledge.
RUFUS: Irrespective of what the inspection finds.
ALEX: Exactly.
JAMIE: Though what the inspection finds is also, you know. Slightly important.
ALEX: Heh. Yes.
RUFUS: We can hold both thoughts.
